replies: Saved: Knows SQL, Excel and Tableau; 2 years of reporting experience. Is that right?

Your skills map well to core data analyst requirements.

Matches (strong):
- SQL — essential for querying databases, joining tables, aggregations and building datasets.
- Excel — key for ad-hoc analysis, pivot tables, VLOOKUP/XLOOKUP, data cleaning and quick modeling.
- Tableau — covers visualization, dashboards and communicating findings to stakeholders.
- 2 years of reporting experience — shows practical use of those tools, working with business metrics and producing regular deliverables.
Gaps you may want to close (common in postings):
- Statistical methods and A/B testing — many analyst roles ask for hypothesis testing, regression or experiment analysis.
- Python or R — useful for deeper analysis, automation and working with larger datasets.
- Data engineering/ETL familiarity — tools or concepts (SQL pipelines, Airflow, dbt) are often asked.
- Product/metric sense and stakeholder storytelling — demonstrate impact with metrics and business outcomes (if not already part of your reporting).

replies:
You have one final round with Lincoln International for an analyst role. Focused, actionable prep below — do these now in order.

What they’ll want, in one line
- Technical rigor (valuation, LBO and comps), clear modeling logic, commercial judgment, and fit: teamwork, client focus and stamina for long hours.

Answer structure to use on every behavioral or fit question
- Situation: one line context
- Task: your responsibility/goal
- Action: 2–3 concrete things you did (tools, numbers, decisions)
- Result: outcome with numbers, timeline, or what you learned
Keep short stories 40–90s; deal walkthroughs 90–150s.
High-value things to prepare (do these now, in this order)
1) Walk me through a deal (your best one)
- 90–120s rehearsed. Say your role first, what you modeled, the valuation range you produced, one sensitivity you ran, and how your work changed the recommendation.

2) Modeling / technical drill
- Be ready to build or talk through a compact 3-statement link and a back-of-envelope LBO: sources & uses, basic debt schedule, exit math and IRR. Practice a 2-minute silent explanation and a 6–8 minute numeric walk-through.

3) Comps and precedent logic
- Explain how you pick comps (business model, size, growth, margin), what adjustments you make, and why you weight a multiple set a certain way.
4) Accounting traps & FCF
- Be able to explain working capital movements, capex vs expense, and how those flow to free cash flow and valuation.

5) Fit and motivation
- Why IB/M&A, why Lincoln, why analyst: two short, specific reasons tied to Lincoln’s mid-market/client exposure and how your experience maps.

Case / problem approach
- State assumptions, show math, give a 1–2 line conclusion, then quick sensitivities. Verbally signpost steps.
Practice questions to run aloud (I can score them if you want)
- “Walk me through your most relevant deal.”  
- “Talk me through an LBO of a business with stable margins.”  
- “How would you value Company X? Which method do you weight most and why?”  
- “Tell me about a time you disagreed with a teammate.”  
- “Why Lincoln International?”  
- “How do you prioritize multiple urgent requests from seniors/clients?”
Two timed drills (do both, strictly timed)
- Drill A — Whiteboard LBO (10 minutes): Purchase multiple, debt multiple, basic amortization, project cashflows, compute exit and IRR. Speak assumptions first, then math, then sensitivity to margin and exit multiple.
- Drill B — Comps choice + short DCF (6 minutes): Given 3 comps with different multiples, defend choice and sketch a simple DCF sensitivity showing where DCF would differ.
Short lines to memorize (one-sentence)
- Why Lincoln: two specific facts about their mid-market/client exposure + how your experience maps. (If you don’t have a specific recent deal, tie to their sector focus and client-facing analyst work.)
- Your technical strength: “My core strength is [modeling/deal execution/valuation], shown by [specific task—e.g., built the 3-statement model and led sensitivity analysis on X deal].”
- Notice/availability: one sentence.
What interviewers listen for (and how to show it)
- Comfort with numbers: speak assumptions, show math, don’t mumble.
- Commercial judgment: give a 1–2 line recommendation and why.
- Teamwork + senior feedback: one example where you incorporated senior input and improved the outcome.
- Energy/stamina: short line on why you want this role long-term.

Delivery fixes (quick)
- Lead with the conclusion in technical answers.
- Verbally signpost (“First assumptions, then returns, then sensitivities”).
- Use numbers early (“6x EBITDA purchase implies $X EV”).
- If you don’t know something, state the assumption and how you’d test it.
30-minute runbook for today (do this exact sequence)
- 0–5m: 30s elevator pitch + 30s “Why Lincoln.”
- 5–20m: mock 1 — deal walkthrough (timebox 5–8m) + mock 2 — LBO build (10m).
- 20–28m: quick behavioral mock: “Tell me about a time you failed.”
- 28–30m: capture 3 closing bullets you’ll leave the interview with (why you, one technical point, availability).

Immediate post-interview checklist
- Send short thank-you notes within 24 hours to each interviewer (I can draft 2-line notes).
- Log interview outcome and any feedback you received — tell me and I’ll record it.
If you want a live drill now
- I’ll ask one interview question and score your answer. Ready to start? (If yes, I’ll ask: “Walk me through your most relevant deal.”)
